text: Every backup and disaster recovery decision in this chapter traces back to two numbers: RTO and RPO. This lesson covers what they actually measure, why they're business decisions rather than technical ones, and a worked example of how they drive your backup schedule instead of the other way around.

RTO, Recovery Time Objective, is how long a system can be down before that downtime becomes genuinely unacceptable. RPO, Recovery Point Objective, is how much data loss is acceptable if you have to restore from a backup, also measured in time. Both come from asking the people who depend on the system, not from what's technically convenient to build.

Here's the worked example. If the business says it can lose at most one hour of order data, that's an RPO of one hour — and that means backups must run at least every sixty minutes, with no exceptions. A once-daily backup job cannot satisfy a one-hour RPO, no matter how reliable that daily job is, because its worst-case data loss is a full day, not an hour.

This is why RTO and RPO get defined before you configure a single backup policy, not after. A team that picks nightly backups first and calls that its strategy has the order backwards — it's chosen a schedule with no idea what RPO it actually delivers. And RTO isn't just the restore time itself; it includes the time to detect the outage and start the restore in the first place.

The two numbers aren't the same kind of number, either. A marketing site might need a tight RTO because being down looks bad, but a loose RPO since losing a day of content edits doesn't hurt much. A nightly batch job might tolerate a loose RTO but demand a tight RPO if it's processing financial transactions. Set both honestly for the specific workload, because the rest of this chapter's backup policy and DR plan get built directly on top of them.
